title: A Simple Way To Improve Student Talk
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses the difficulty many teachers face getting students engaged in quality classroom discussion, noting that increased pressure and pushing for participation tends to backfire, causing students to clam up rather than open up. His proposed fix is a low-stakes, five-minute warm-up activity done before a lesson: students stand in pairs or groups and discuss a fun, low-pressure prompt (like describing a favorite place or imagining being a superhero) purely for enjoyment, without grading or formal expectations. Linsin argues this loosens students up, builds comfort with sharing and listening, and by the second or third round produces the animated, engaged conversation teachers are hoping to cultivate—benefits that then carry over into the actual academic discussion that follows.
points: Pressuring students to talk more or perform in discussions tends to freeze them up rather than free them to communicate.
The recommended fix is a five-minute pre-lesson warm-up: students stand in pairs or groups and discuss a fun, ungraded prompt purely for enjoyment.
Standing during the activity is intended to increase energy and readiness, distinct from a formal academic discussion.
By the second or third round of practice, the informal conversational energy begins to resemble the engaged discussion the teacher is hoping to cultivate.
The core insight is that natural, spontaneous conversation cannot be manufactured through pressure—it requires freedom and enjoyment first.
quotes: Are you having trouble getting your students engaged in quality discussions? You’re not alone.
But when students feel pressure, they clam up. It freezes their brain rather than frees their brain.
Natural, spontaneous conversations can never be manufactured. They can’t be forced, dictated, or even strongly encouraged.
Standing gets the blood going, shakes the cobwebs free, and prepares them for action.
By the second or third round, the conversation will begin to reflect what you’ve been working so hard to achieve. Your students will be animated and energetic.
You see, it’s supposed to be enjoyable. It’s why we meet friends for coffee or talk on the phone for an hour and a half.
